contents: I spent the last few months building three small but real backends — a webhook relay, an internal admin API, and a rate-limited proxy — each in a different Rust web framework, on purpose. Not a toy benchmark, actual services with auth, database pools, and traffic. The goal was simple: figure out which Rust web framework I’d actually reach for by default in 2026, and which ones only make sense in specific situations.
title: Rust for Web Backends in 2026: Axum vs Actix vs Rocket

contents: I used to think good architecture was a taste thing — something senior engineers cared about and everyone else tolerated. Then I started letting an AI agent write 70% of my code, and within two weeks I understood exactly why architecture existed in the first place. Not as a rulebook. As the only thing standing between “the agent shipped a working feature” and “the agent shipped a working feature that quietly wired the payment service directly into the UI layer.
title: Clean Architecture in the Age of AI-Generated Code: Why Structure Matters More Than Ever in 2026

contents: Every C++ standard since C++11 has been “the incremental one” — C++17 tidied things up, C++20 gave us concepts and coroutines, C++23 was mostly cleanup. C++26 is different. Two features landing in it — static reflection and contracts — have been on the wishlist since before C++11 shipped, and they’re finally real. I went through the accepted papers and current compiler support to figure out what actually changes for people writing C++ day to day, not just what sounds impressive on a slide.
title: What's Coming in C++26: Reflection, Contracts, and the Biggest Standard Update in Years

contents: A few months back I had a Node service that was randomly stalling for a couple hundred milliseconds every few minutes. No exceptions, no error logs, nothing in the APM dashboard worth screenshotting. Application-level tracing was useless because the problem wasn’t in the application — it was somewhere between the syscall layer and the disk. The tool that actually cracked it open wasn’t a new logging library or a fancier metrics agent.
title: eBPF in 2026: The Linux Superpower Every Backend Developer Should Understand

contents: Every October brings a new CPython release and every October I skim the changelog, shrug, and move on — most releases are incremental. Python 3.14 is not one of those years. Between free-threaded Python losing its “experimental” label, a genuinely new string type, and subinterpreters finally becoming usable from plain Python code, this is the first release in a while where I actually rewrote some of my own code after reading the changelog.
title: Python 3.14: New Features Every Developer Should Know in 2026

contents: Every few months another vector database shows up with a slick landing page and a Series A. Meanwhile the database most of us already run in production quietly picked up everything it needed to do the same job. I spent the last couple of weeks moving a small RAG prototype off a dedicated vector store and onto plain PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, mostly out of curiosity about whether it would actually hold up.
title: PostgreSQL 18 and pgvector: Building AI-Native Applications on Postgres in 2026

contents: I’ve shipped the same login screen twice — once in Kotlin for Android, once in Swift for iOS — more times than I’d like to admit. Same validation rules, same API calls, same retry logic, written twice, tested twice, and inevitably drifting apart the moment one platform gets a bugfix the other doesn’t. Kotlin Multiplatform was supposed to fix that, and for a long time it felt like a promising side project more than a real answer.
title: Kotlin Multiplatform in 2026: Sharing Code Between Android and iOS Without Compromise

contents: Every time I open a new tab it’s another SaaS wrapper around someone else’s API key. contents: Every “how to build an AI agent” tutorial teaches you one loop and stops there. What I kept missing was the thing every other corner of software engineering already has: a catalog. contents: I spent last week migrating a legacy RecyclerView screen to Compose, and about halfway through I realized I wasn’t doing it because I felt like it anymore — I was doing it because Google just told the entire Android ecosystem that Views is no longer where new work happens. That’s a bigger deal than another Compose point release, so I want to walk through what actually changed at I/O 2026, what’s new in Compose 1.
title: Jetpack Compose Goes Compose-First in 2026: What Android Developers Need to Know

contents: I spent a chunk of last week ripping JavaScript out of a component library. Not because it was buggy — because it didn’t need to exist anymore. A resize observer that toggled a class based on container width, a form validation script that just added an “invalid” class to a parent div, a PostCSS plugin that faked layer-like ordering — all three jobs are now native CSS. This post is a walkthrough of the three features that made that possible: container queries, :has(), and cascade layers, plus native nesting and scroll-driven animations along the way, with real code for each.
title: Modern CSS in 2026: Container Queries, :has(), and Cascade Layers

contents:

contents:
Every “build an AI agent” tutorial I ran into lately starts with pip install langchain or pip install langgraph. Useful tools, but they hide the actual mechanism. Before reaching for a framework, I wanted to see the loop with my own eyes — so I built the smallest working agent I could, in plain Python.

Six months ago “vibe coding” meant typing a vague prompt and hoping the output compiled. I did it. It worked until it didn’t — the moment a codebase got past toy-project size, prompt-and-hope fell apart. What replaced it, quietly, wasn’t a better prompt. It was a different job description.
The shift nobody announced I still write code every day. I just don’t type most of it anymore. The work moved up a level: instead of implementing a function, I write a spec for what the function needs to do, constraints it has to respect, and then I watch an agent build it.

The std::set container in C++ is part of the Standard Template Library (STL) and is used to store unique elements in a sorted order.
It’s a powerful associative container when you need quick lookups, automatic sorting, and no duplicate values.
    Watch on YouTube    Key Characteristics  Stores only unique elements (duplicates are not allowed). Sorted order of elements (by default, ascending). Fast search, insertion, and deletion — average O(log n) complexity.

In C++, classes have three access modifiers that determine the level of access to class members. These are: public, private, and protected.
Private and protected members are accessible only within the class and its subclasses, whereas public members are accessible anywhere.
Private members are declared with the private keyword in the class definition. Private members cannot be accessed outside of the class or its friend functions. This means that only the members of the class or its friend functions can access them.

In C++, a pure virtual function is a virtual function that is declared in a base class but does not provide an implementation.
Syntax: virtual return_type functionName(parameters) = 0; Where  = 0  at the end of the declaration indicates that the function is pure virtual.
A class that contains one or more pure virtual functions is called an abstract class, and it cannot be instantiated (can not create an object for this class).
title: Pure Virtual Functions

When a virtual function is called on a derived class object, the function of the derived class is called instead of the function of the base class. This is known as dynamic binding or runtime polymorphism.
Syntax: virtual return_type functionName() { //body of the function  return statement; } Suppose we have a base class named Shape and three derived classes named Circle and Rectangle and Triangle.
